newsitem.title: UK: Clogged arteries linked with Alzheimer's - study.
newsitem.headline: Clogged arteries linked with Alzheimer's - study.

text.p: Dutch and Belgian researchers reported on Friday they had found clear evidence linking Alzheimer's disease, the most common form of dementia, with clogged arteries.
They said Alzheimer's patients were more likely to have atherosclerosis -- fat clogging the arteries -- and also said a blood protein known as apolipoprotein-E had a strong role.

Albert Hofman of Erasmus University in Rotterdam and colleagues at the University of Antwerp studied 284 patients with dementia, most of them with Alzheimer's, against 1,700 volunteers who did not have it.
"All indicators of atherosclerosis were associated with dementia," they wrote in the Lancet medical journal.
The worse the atherosclerosis, the more cases there were of dementia.
Clogged arteries have been linked with dementia in the past. Doctors say this is not surprising, as atherosclerosis can reduce blood flow to the brain.
But Hofman's group said no one had singled out Alzheimer's before.

Hofman's group also tested the DNA from most of the patients and found those who suffered dementia were more likely to carry a certain gene controlling production of apolipoprotein-E, which is known to be associated with Alzheimer's.

"These findings suggest that dementia and its two major subtypes, Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia, are associated with atherosclerosis and that there is an interaction between apolipoprotein-E and atherosclerosis in...Alzheimer's disease," they concluded.
Apolipoprotein-E is associated with the transport of fat in the blood. The body packages fat into parcels known as lipoproteins for easy movement.
